household.name: casket wall, panel, burial box
household.title: casket wall, panel, burial box
household.reason: Two carved and painted cedar panels forming the walls of a mortuary/burial box, decorated in classic Northwest Coast formline style with crest imagery (eyes, ovoids, faces); such painted grave boxes are documented Tsimshian mortuary art collected on the Retzius 1893 North America expedition.

household.name: basket
household.title: basket
household.reason: A tightly woven twined basket with a stylized human face design in imbricated/false-embroidery technique, attributed to the Tsimshian/Northwest Coast Peoples — a classic form of basketry made and used by this culture.

household.name: hammer
household.title: hammer
household.reason: A carved stone maul head with a zoomorphic (salmon/whale) crest and grooves for hafting—this is a characteristic Northwest Coast stone hammer/maul tool type, consistent with Tsimshian material culture.

household.name: bowl, vessel, trough, bowl
household.title: bowl, vessel, trough, bowl
household.reason: This is a carved wooden grease/oil dish inlaid with opercula shells along the rim, a classic Northwest Coast vessel type used by Tsimshian and neighboring peoples for serving oolichan or other oils, consistent with the claimed ethnicity.

household.name: fiskkrok
household.title: fiskkrok
household.reason: The object is a wooden halibut hook (v-shaped, carved, with barb), explicitly a type used by Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian peoples of the northern Northwest Coast; the museum text itself even labels it "Tlingit" but confirms this hook form was shared by all three groups, supporting the Tsimshian claim as plausible.

household.name: tool/implement; weight
household.title: tool/implement; weight (net?)
household.reason: A carved stone zoomorphic object (likely a net weight/tool) attributed to the Tsimshian of the Northwest Coast; such small carved stone effigy tools are consistent with Northwest Coast material culture and the maker attribution is specific (not merely "style").

household.name: jar
household.title: jar
household.reason: This is a twined cedarbark basket with false-embroidery designs covering a glass jar, made by the Tsimshian — a household woven container, not ceramic.

household.name: weaving-frame; strap
household.title: weaving-frame; strap
household.reason: A wooden weaving frame with a partially woven band strap attached, attributed to the Tsimshian (Northwest Coast Peoples) — a plausible traditional weaving tool from this culture.

household.name: hammer
household.title: hammer
household.reason: A grooved stone maul/hammer with an old collection label reading "Stone hammer Fort Simpson," which is documented Coast Tsimshian territory, consistent with the museum's Tsimshian (Coast) attribution.

arms.name: club
arms.title: club
arms.reason: An elkhorn war club with a bird-head pommel inlaid with haliotis shell, a classic Northwest Coast weapon type attributed to the Tsimshian by the museum.

arms.name: klubba, club
arms.title: klubba, club
arms.reason: A stone-headed club with wooden haft, attributed by the museum's general catalogue to British Columbia and identified as a type used by Northwest Coast peoples, consistent with Tsimshian material culture.

arms.name: klubba, club
arms.title: klubba, club
arms.reason: A stone club head carved with an animal face (eyes, lips, teeth) is a classic Northwest Coast stone weapon type, provenanced to British Columbia; consistent with Tsimshian or neighboring Northwest Coast peoples, who cannot be reliably distinguished by style alone.

arms.name: klubba, club
arms.title: klubba, club
arms.reason: A stone-headed club with wood haft, collected in British Columbia on the 1898 Alaska/Klondike expedition, a plausible Northwest Coast (Tsimshian) household/war implement, though the museum itself calls it likely a household tool rather than a weapon.

arms.name: klubba, club
arms.title: klubba, club
arms.reason: A stone-headed war club with wooden shaft lashed with sinew, described as a Northwest Coast club type (British Columbia provenance) used by Northwest Coast Indians historically and into modern times; this is a plausible Tsimshian weapon type.

arms.name: klubba, club
arms.title: klubba, club
arms.reason: The image shows a stone club/maul head carved with a salmon-head motif, a well-documented Northwest Coast Indian weapon type found with British Columbia provenance — the exact form associated with Tsimshian and neighboring coastal groups, and plausible for this culture.

masks-ritual.name: head-dress
masks-ritual.title: head-dress
masks-ritual.reason: A shaman's headdress made of goat horns and leather with a bronze wire headband, attributed to the Tsimshian (Northwest Coast Peoples) — a wearable ritual item made and used by this group.

masks-ritual.name: mask
masks-ritual.title: mask
masks-ritual.reason: A carved wooden articulated bird-head mask with movable lower jaw worked by strings, a classic Northwest Coast transformation-mask type attributed to the Tsimshian, consistent with the museum's attribution.

masks-ritual.name: file; wand; amulet
masks-ritual.title: file (?); wand (?); amulet (?)
masks-ritual.reason: A carved stone object (possibly amulet/wand) showing formline-style crest carving of a fish (sturgeon) with a human face on the tail and a sea-mammal head at the other end, attributed directly to Tsimshian makers — a ritual/crest object consistent with Northwest Coast Tsimshian tradition.

masks-ritual.name: prydnad
masks-ritual.title: prydnad
masks-ritual.reason: This is a carved wooden headdress frontlet fragment (likely a beaver figure below, bird/animal form above) inlaid with abalone shell, in Northwest Coast style from British Columbia — consistent with Tsimshian ceremonial headdress art, though damaged. It is not jewelry but a ritual/regalia object.

masks-ritual.name: head-dress
masks-ritual.title: head-dress
masks-ritual.reason: A woven fibre headdress mounted with goat/mountain horns, attributed to the Tsimshian as a shaman's ceremonial headdress worn for a "dog feast" — this is a worn ritual object consistent with Northwest Coast Tsimshian practice, though the museum notes it is "said to be fake."

garment.name: Blanket
garment.title: Dance Cape, known as a Button Blanket
garment.reason: This is a classic Northwest Coast button blanket/dance cape with a crest figure outlined in mother-of-pearl shell buttons on wool trade cloth, a form made and worn by Tsimshian and neighboring Northwest Coast peoples for ceremonial regalia.

garment.name: hat
garment.title: hat
garment.reason: A twined cedar bark wide-brimmed hat, a classic Northwest Coast woven garment attributed to Tsimshian makers, matching the museum's production credit.

sculpture.name: Frontlet
sculpture.title: Headdress Frontlet
sculpture.reason: This is a carved wooden frontlet with abalone shell inlay depicting an ancestral/crest figure, worn on Northwest Coast headdresses — a well-documented Tsimshian regalia form. It was mis-filed as jewelry but clearly belongs to the culture.

sculpture.name: print
sculpture.title: print
sculpture.reason: The image is a printed photograph of a carved cedar Tsimshian storage chest with a conventionalized sea lion design, an object made and used by the Tsimshian. It's a documentary reproduction (print of a photo) rather than an original artwork, so architectural-style/sculpture classification aside, it depicts a genuine Tsimshian carved object.

sculpture.name: totempåle, fotografi, photograph
sculpture.title: totempåle, fotografi, photograph
sculpture.reason: The image shows carved Northwest Coast totem poles (with crest figures like a beaver/bear holding a figure) photographed on display at the Smithsonian; the museum's own caption identifies it as a Tsimshian totem pole, consistent with Tsimshian carving traditions.

photo.name: trumma, hövding, mask, fotografi, photograph
photo.title: trumma, hövding, mask, fotografi, photograph
photo.reason: The photograph shows a group of chiefs and family members in ceremonial regalia (frontlets, Chilkat-style robes, fur mantles) surrounded by masks and a crest-painted chest and panel, identified by the museum as Coast Tsimshian, photographed at Gitladamix among Nisga'a/Tsimshian wolf-clan chiefs — this is documentary photography of Tsimshian ceremonial dress and material culture.

jewelry.name: frontlet
jewelry.title: frontlet
jewelry.reason: This is a carved wooden frontlet inlaid with abalone shell, depicting a crest figure with a humanoid face, sea lion whiskers, and ermine-style attachments — a classic Northwest Coast chief's headdress ornament attributed to the Tsimshian.

jewelry.name: bracelet
jewelry.title: bracelet
jewelry.reason: Silver cuff bracelet engraved with a Thunderbird in Northwest Coast formline style, signed by the artist, and attributed by the museum to a Tsimshian maker — a classic Northwest Coast jewelry form.

jewelry.name: head-ring; crown
jewelry.title: head-ring; crown
jewelry.reason: A woven bark/fibre head-ring or crown worn as ceremonial regalia, attributed by the museum to the Tsimshian; this is a plausible traditional adornment made and worn by the people.

jewelry.name: bracelet
jewelry.title: bracelet
jewelry.reason: A silver cuff bracelet engraved with a formline frog design, signed by a Northwest Coast artist and attributed by the museum to Tsimshian make — a classic Northwest Coast jewelry form.

instruments.name: Raven rattle
instruments.title: Raven rattle
instruments.reason: A carved and painted wooden Raven rattle with classic Northwest Coast formline design, a canonical Tsimshian chief's ceremonial instrument used in dance.

instruments.name: clapper
instruments.title: clapper
instruments.reason: A wooden whale-shaped ceremonial clapper with formline black and red painted designs, a traditional Northwest Coast Tsimshian ritual musical instrument, clearly matching known Tsimshian craft.

instruments.name: flute; clapper
instruments.title: flute (?); clapper (?)
instruments.reason: A wooden hollowed instrument (flute or clapper), a plausible traditional wind/percussion instrument type for Northwest Coast peoples like the Tsimshian.

instruments.name: trumpet, aerophone
instruments.title: trumpet, aerophone
instruments.reason: A carved wooden trumpet/aerophone with incised decoration, a type used by Tsimshian (and neighboring Kwakiutl, Haida) groups in secret society performances; museum notes explicitly attribute this instrument type to Tsimshian use.

instruments.name: Rattle
instruments.title: Face Rattle
instruments.reason: A carved wooden face rattle with articulated jaw, characteristic of Northwest Coast ceremonial regalia including Tsimshian shamanic and dance rattles, matching the claimed ethnicity, category, and mid-19th-century date.
